subject: math
objective: Explain why a geometric series with |r| < 1 has a finite sum (the gap to a/(1 − r) is multiplied by r at every step); derive the partial-sum formula S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) by shifting and subtracting; decide convergence from the common ratio; and, given a geometric series in sigma notation with any starting index, find its first term, common ratio, and sum or state that it diverges.
prerequisites: Limit of a sequence, including r^n → 0 when |r| < 1
sources: OpenStax, Calculus Volume 2, Section 5.2: Infinite Series, subsection Geometric Series and Example 5.10 (repeating decimals) (https://openstax.org/books/calculus-volume-2/pages/5-2-infinite-series)

OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, Section 3.5: Free Fall, for y = y0 + v0·t − ½gt² with v0 = 0 and g ≈ 9.8 m/s², giving fall time √(2h/g) (https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/3-5-free-fall)
misconceptions: Adding infinitely many positive numbers must give infinity
The first term a is the coefficient in front of the power, regardless of the starting index
The ratio is first term ÷ second term (upside down)
A negative ratio means the series diverges, or the sign of r can be dropped
a/(1 − r) gives the sum for any r, including |r| ≥ 1 (e.g. 1 + 2 + 4 + ⋯ = −1)
A series whose partial sums stay bounded must converge (r = −1)
The infinite sum is something you reach after enough terms, rather than a limit of partial sums
modelLimitations: Partial sums in the explorer are computed in floating point and shown rounded; the target and practice answers use exact fractions.
The ratio slider moves in steps of 0.05 (plus exact presets such as 1/3 and 2/3), and the first term is limited to 1 to 4.
The derivation uses n from 3 to 6 and a short list of ratios so the columns fit on screen; the text says the cancellation holds for every n.
Practice problems are randomly generated from nine convergent templates and two divergent ones; series that need splitting into two geometric series or have a variable x are not included.
Decimal answers within 0.0005 of the exact value are accepted, with the exact value shown.
The bouncing-ball model ignores air resistance, uses g = 9.8 m/s², and assumes a constant bounce ratio and infinitely many bounces; real balls stop after finitely many.
Picture proofs cover r = 1/2 and r = 1/4 only.
